quizzes.title: Key terms across the lectures
quizzes.intro: Words used in the costing of dyeing, finishing and stitching.

questions.q: A process route is
options: The road from mill to port
The sequence of machines a fabric passes through
The path of the weft through the shed
questions.explain: For example: bleaching, then pad-steam dyeing, then stenter. Each step adds its cost per metre.

questions.q: The bottleneck of a finishing plant is
options: The machine with the highest speed
The machine whose capacity limits the output of the whole plant
questions.explain: The plant can produce no more than its slowest necessary stage allows.

questions.q: Set-up time on a dyeing range is time spent
options: Cleaning and preparing between orders, producing nothing
Waiting for the customer to pay
questions.explain: During set-up the machine earns nothing but its fixed cost continues.

questions.q: “Gross grey price per finished metre” allows for
questions.explain: More than one metre of grey is needed for each finished metre, so the grey price is divided by (1 − loss).

questions.q: Linear rating in stitching is
options: Metres of fabric consumed by one piece
questions.explain: It is the cut length along the roll, in metres, for one sheet or pillow case.

questions.q: Rags in a stitching order are
options: Leftover fabric sold for a small credit
questions.explain: Cutting leftovers bring in a little money, which is deducted from fabric cost.

questions.q: Routine accessories such as thread, labels and polybags are part of the variable cost of a made-up item.
questions.explain: They are used piece by piece, so their cost rises with the number of pieces.

questions.q: Shade depth affects dyeing cost mainly through
options: The cost of dyes and chemicals per metre
questions.explain: A dark shade needs far more dye than a light one: Rs 15 or 25 per metre against Rs 3 in the lecture.

questions.q: In the stitching lecture, fixed cost is charged to each item as
options: A multiple of its direct labour
A rate per metre of fabric
questions.explain: Fixed cost is absorbed at 3.2 × direct labour, so labour-heavy items carry more overhead.

questions.q: Cold pad batch dyeing is the cheapest route in the lecture and therefore the best choice for every order.
questions.explain: It is slow, ties fabric up during batching and suits reactive dyes only. Route choice also depends on quality and delivery.

quizzes.title: Linking the ideas
quizzes.intro: How order size, routes and percentages change the cost of a metre or a piece.

questions.q: Commission and export surcharge are percentages of proceeds. To include them in a quotation you should
options: Add the same percentage to cost
Divide the required proceeds by (1 − the percentages)
questions.explain: They are taken from the selling price, not from cost, so the price must be grossed up by division.

questions.q: When order size falls from 10,000 m to 2,000 m, the set-up cost per metre
questions.explain: The same set-up is spread over one fifth of the metres.

questions.q: A route cost is found by
options: Taking the cost of the most expensive process
Adding the cost per metre of each process in the route
questions.explain: Each machine the fabric passes through adds its own cost per metre.

questions.q: Calculated efficiency of a continuous machine for one run is
questions.explain: Only the running minutes produce fabric; the set-up minutes are lost.

questions.q: A fabric passes twice through the same range (dye, then wash). For that fabric the range’s capacity is
questions.explain: Every metre uses the machine twice, so only half as many metres can be finished.

questions.q: Fixed cost per minute is charged for run and set-up minutes, but utilities only for run minutes, because
options: Steam, power and water are used mainly when fabric is running
Fixed cost stops when the machine stops
questions.explain: Depreciation, finance and labour continue all the time; utilities follow the running of the machine.

questions.q: If the fabric is wide enough for a sheet to be cut across the width (“inverted”), the cut length along the roll is based on
options: The finished width plus side margins
questions.explain: The sheet is turned, so the roll is consumed by the width of the sheet instead of its length.

questions.q: Because fixed cost is absorbed on direct labour, small labour-heavy items such as pillow cases carry a heavy share of overhead.
questions.explain: This is why every pillow item in the lecture’s order shows a loss while the comforters carry the order.

questions.q: Spreading a machine’s yearly capital cost over fewer effective metres per hour (lower efficiency) makes the capital cost per metre
questions.explain: The same hourly cost is divided by fewer metres.

questions.q: B-grade fabric from processing gives a credit that reduces the cost of the good dyed fabric.
questions.explain: It is sold at a fraction of the grey price, and that money is deducted from the processing cost.

quizzes.title: Mixed calculations
quizzes.intro: Quotation, capacity and consumption calculations with new figures.

questions.q: Grey fabric costs Rs 120 a metre and 8% is lost in processing. What is the gross grey price per finished metre, to two decimals?
A route is bleaching Rs 3.00, mercerizing Rs 14.00, pad-steam dyeing Rs 10.00 and stenter Rs 7.00 per metre. What is the route cost per metre?
questions.explain: 3 + 14 + 10 + 7 = Rs 34 per metre.

questions.q: A machine costs €2,000,000 and is depreciated over 10 years, with a financial cost of 10% of the machine cost each year. What is the total capital cost per year in euros?
questions.explain: Depreciation 200,000 + finance 200,000 = € 400,000 a year.

questions.q: A range runs at 120 m/min at 80% efficiency. How many metres does it process in an hour?
questions.explain: 120 × 60 × 0.8 = 5,760 metres an hour.

questions.q: A run of 12,000 m at 60 m/min needs 100 minutes of set-up. What is the calculated efficiency, in percent to one decimal?
A machine runs at 40 m/min with a net efficiency of 60%. What is its capacity in metres per day of 24 hours?
Total cost is Rs 150.00 a metre and the exporter wants a 5% margin on cost. Commission and surcharge total 1.25% of proceeds. What price per metre must be quoted, to two decimals?
questions.explain: Required proceeds = 157.50; ÷ 0.9875 = Rs 159.49.

questions.q: The cut length of a sheet along the roll is 98.4 inches. What is the linear rating in metres, to two decimals? (1 m = 39.37 in)
A piece has a linear rating of 2.50 m and 5% wastage is allowed. What is the final rating, to three decimals?
Direct labour on an item is Rs 6.00 a piece and fixed cost is absorbed at 3.2 × direct labour. What is the fixed cost per piece, to two decimals?

quizzes.title: Case study
quizzes.intro: One dyeing range, two order sizes: see how the cost per metre is built and why it changes.

questions.q: For an order of 10,000 metres, how many minutes does the machine run?
For an order of 10,000 metres, what is the calculated efficiency (run time ÷ total time), in percent to one decimal?
For an order of 10,000 metres, what is the machine’s total fixed cost for the order?
questions.explain: 290 minutes × Rs 120 = Rs 34,800.

questions.q: For an order of 10,000 metres, what is the fixed cost per metre, to two decimals?
For an order of 10,000 metres, what is the utilities cost per metre, to two decimals?
questions.explain: 200 minutes × 50 = 10,000; ÷ 10,000 m = Rs 1.00 per metre.

questions.q: For an order of 10,000 metres, what is the dyes cost per metre including the set-up colour, to two decimals?
For an order of 10,000 metres, what is the total dyeing cost per metre (fixed, utilities and dyes), to two decimals?
For an order of only 2,000 metres, what is the fixed cost per metre, to two decimals?
questions.explain: Run 40 min + set-up 90 min = 130 min × 120 = 15,600; ÷ 2,000 = Rs 7.80 per metre.

questions.q: For an order of only 2,000 metres, what is the total dyeing cost per metre, to two decimals?
questions.explain: Fixed 7.80 + utilities 1.00 + dyes 9.20 = Rs 18.00, against 12.72 for the 10,000 m order.

questions.q: Why does the 2,000 metre order cost so much more per metre?
options: The machine runs slower on small orders
The same set-up minutes and set-up colour are spread over fewer metres
Medium shades cost more on small orders
questions.explain: Set-up time and set-up colour are the same for any order, so their cost per metre rises as the order shrinks.

quizzes.case: A thermosol dyeing range runs at 50 metres a minute. Every order needs 90 minutes of set-up (cleaning, preparation and shade matching). The machine’s fixed cost is Rs 120 a minute whether it is running or being set up, and utilities cost Rs 50 a minute while it runs. Dyes for a medium shade cost Rs 8 per metre, and each order also uses set-up colour worth 300 metres.

quizzes.title: Group challenge
quizzes.intro: Quotations and judgement calls across the dyeing and stitching lectures.

questions.q: Local grey costs Rs 100 a metre and 10% is lost in processing, so 1 ÷ 0.90 metres of grey are needed for each finished metre. B-grade equal to 5% of the grey is recovered and sold at 40% of the grey price. What is the B-grade credit per finished metre, to two decimals?
questions.explain: 5% × 40% × 100 = 2.00 per grey metre; ÷ 0.90 = Rs 2.22 per finished metre.

questions.q: A bleaching range has a capital cost of Rs 4,000 an hour and processes 6,250 effective metres an hour. Chemicals cost Rs 1.20 and utilities Rs 1.16 per metre. What is the bleaching cost per metre, to two decimals?
questions.explain: Capital 0.64 + chemicals 1.20 + utilities 1.16 = Rs 3.00 per metre.

questions.q: A plant has these daily capacities: bleaching 138,000 m, mercerizing 57,600 m, thermosol 34,000 m, stenter 92,000 m. If all fabric must pass through every machine, the plant’s capacity is about
questions.explain: The slowest necessary machine, the thermosol range, sets the limit for the whole line.

questions.q: A thermosol range has a capacity of 34,000 m a day for a single pass. How many metres a day can it finish of a fabric that needs a double pass?
questions.explain: Each metre uses the machine twice: 34,000 ÷ 2 = 17,000 metres.

questions.q: A pillow case order: 1,776 A-grade pieces at a linear rating of 0.43 m, plus 4.30 m in B-grade pieces and 25 m of rags. How many metres of fabric are consumed, to two decimals?

An item costs Rs 74.50 in fabric (net of credits), Rs 10.00 in accessories and Rs 1.20 in direct labour per piece; fixed cost is 3.2 × direct labour. What is the total cost per piece, to two decimals?
An order has eight items. Two comforter lines make Rs 270,000 profit and six small items lose Rs 30,000 between them. The best conclusion is
options: The order is profitable, so every price is fine
Small items should be priced on their own cost, not carried by the comforters
Fixed cost should not be charged at all
questions.explain: A total hides cross-subsidy. Each item should be judged, and quoted, on its own cost.

questions.q: Choosing a shorter route for a shade always gives the same fabric quality at lower cost.
questions.explain: Routes differ in fastness, appearance, dye class and delivery time. Cost is one input to the decision, not the only one.

questions.q: A sheet is cut with a length of 110 inches along the roll. With 5% wastage, what is the final rating in metres, to two decimals? (1 m = 39.37 in)
Which change would reduce the dyeing cost per metre of small orders the most?
options: Grouping small orders of the same shade so that one set-up serves several
Using a lighter shade for all customers
questions.explain: Set-up is the cost that hurts short runs. Sharing one set-up across several orders spreads it over more metres.
